blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 11 (Human Circulatory System), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.
11.1 Structure and functioning of the heart

blocks.prompt: 1 What is blood? Name its two main components with their share by volume.
blocks.explanation: Blood is the medium in which dissolved nutrients, gases, hormones and wastes are transported throughout the body. Its components: plasma (about 55% by volume) and cells or cell-like bodies, i.e. white blood cells, red blood cells and platelets (about 45%).

book_ref.quote: It is composed of two main components (i) plasma

blocks.prompt: 2 Give reason: the heart is usually felt on the left side although it lies in the middle of the chest.
blocks.explanation: The heart lies in the middle of the chest between the lungs, but its left side is stronger and larger because it pumps blood to all body parts. So the heartbeat is felt more on the left; the left lung is smaller and has a cardiac notch for the heart.

book_ref.quote: The heart is usually felt to be on the left side

blocks.prompt: 3 What is pericardium? Name its layers.
blocks.explanation: Pericardium is the sac enclosing the heart, separating it from surrounding organs. Layers: outer fibrous pericardium (strong connective tissue) and inner serous pericardium, which has an outer parietal pericardium and an inner visceral pericardium (epicardium).

book_ref.quote: Pericardium separates heart from surrounding organs.

blocks.prompt: 4 Where is pericardial fluid found? Write its functions.
blocks.explanation: Pericardial fluid (up to 50 mL) is found in the pericardial cavity, the space between the parietal and visceral pericardium. It lubricates the heart and protects it from infections.

book_ref.quote: It lubricates heart and protects it from infections.

blocks.prompt: 5 Differentiate between epicardium and endocardium.
blocks.explanation: Both are layers of the heart wall, with the myocardium between them.

book_ref.quote: The inner layer of pericardium i.e., epicardium makes the outer lining of heart wall.

rows: Outer lining of the heart wall
Inner lining of the heart chambers
It is the inner (visceral) layer of the pericardium
A single layer of epithelial cells
Lies above the myocardium
Lies beneath the myocardium

blocks.prompt: 6 Differentiate between atria and ventricles.
blocks.explanation: Both are chambers of the heart.

book_ref.quote: Atria receive blood from body and pass it to ventricles

rows: Two upper chambers
Two lower chambers
Thin-walled
Thick-walled
Receive blood and pass it to the ventricles
Distribute blood to the body
Separated by the interatrial septum
Separated by the much thicker interventricular septum

blocks.prompt: 7 Why is the human heart called a double pump?
blocks.explanation: Because it carries out two circulations: pulmonary circulation (supply of blood to the lungs) by the right side and systemic circulation (supply of blood to all organs except lungs) by the left side.

book_ref.quote: Human heart functions as a double pump.

blocks.prompt: 8 Which side of the heart contains oxygenated blood and which side deoxygenated blood?
blocks.explanation: The right side of the heart contains deoxygenated blood (from the body, going to the lungs) and the left side contains oxygenated blood (from the lungs, going to the body). Complete separation of the two is maintained.

book_ref.quote: Complete separation of deoxygenated (right side) and oxygenated (left side) blood is maintained in heart.

blocks.prompt: 9 Define cardiac cycle. How long does each part of it last?
blocks.explanation: The alternating relaxations and contractions of the heart chambers are together called a cardiac cycle or one heartbeat. Diastole lasts about 0.4 s, atrial systole about 0.1 s and ventricular systole about 0.3 s.

book_ref.quote: Its alternating relaxations and contractions are collectively called a cardiac cycle

blocks.prompt: 10 Differentiate between 'lubb' and 'dubb' sounds of the heart.
blocks.explanation: Both are heart sounds heard with a stethoscope.

book_ref.quote: When both ventricles contract simultaneously to pump the blood

rows: Made when the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close
Made when the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves close
Produced when both ventricles contract (start of ventricular systole)
Produced when ventricular systole ends and the ventricles relax

blocks.prompt: 11 What is a heart murmur? How are serious cases corrected?
blocks.explanation: If the heart valves do not close fully or open narrowly, turbulence is created in the heart; it is heard as a murmur, which sounds like a hiss. Serious murmurs can be corrected by replacing damaged valves with artificial ones or with valves from an organ donor.

book_ref.quote: This turbulence can be heard as a heart murmur.

blocks.prompt: 12 What is the SA node? Why is it called the pacemaker?
blocks.explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node is a small cluster of cardiac muscle cells embedded in the upper wall of the right atrium. It is called the pacemaker because it initiates the pumping of the heart: it sends electrical impulses to the atrial walls, making both atria contract.

book_ref.quote: The pumping of heart is initiated by the Sinoatrial Node (SA node) or pacemaker.

blocks.prompt: 13 What is the bundle of His? Write its role.
blocks.explanation: The bundle of His (atrioventricular bundle) is a network of fibres in the interventricular septum. It receives impulses from the AV node and divides into left and right branches ending at the Purkinje fibres, so the ventricles contract almost simultaneously.

book_ref.quote: From AV node, the impulses reach an atrioventricular bundle or bundle of His.

blocks.prompt: 14 Give reason: impulses are delayed between the SA node and the AV node.
blocks.explanation: There is a delay of about 0.15 second in conduction from the SA node to the AV node. It lets atrial systole be completed before ventricular systole begins, so the ventricles are filled before they contract.

book_ref.quote: permitting atrial systole to be completed before ventricular systole begins

blocks.prompt: 15 What is an artificial pacemaker? When is it used?
blocks.explanation: An artificial pacemaker is a battery-operated device placed surgically in the body. It emits electrical signals that trigger normal heartbeats. It is used when the SA node is weak or impulses are blocked, which may delay or stop the heartbeat.

book_ref.quote: It emits electrical signals that trigger normal heartbeats.

blocks.prompt: 16 How does the brain change the heart rate?
blocks.explanation: The normal rate (about 70 per minute) is set by the pacemaker and AV node. During fever and exercise the brain's control centre sends nerve signals to both, increasing the heart rate; during sleep or rest it slows their activity.

book_ref.quote: Brain also exerts some influence on heart rate.

blocks.prompt: 17 Differentiate between the P wave and the T wave of an ECG.
blocks.explanation: Both are waves of a normal ECG.

book_ref.quote: T wave abnormalities may indicate electrolyte disturbance.

rows: Shows the beginning of atrial depolarization, initiated by the SA node
Represents the beginning of repolarization of ventricles
Causes atrial contraction
Comes after the ST segment
Irregular or absent P waves may indicate arrhythmia
Abnormalities may indicate electrolyte disturbance; a hyper-acute T wave is an early sign of acute myocardial infarction

blocks.prompt: 18 What is the QT interval? What is its normal value?
blocks.explanation: The QT interval of an ECG is measured from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave. A normal QT interval is usually about 0.40 seconds.

book_ref.quote: The QT interval is from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave.

blocks.prompt: 19 What does the ST segment show? What do its changes indicate?
blocks.explanation: The ST segment shows the completion of depolarization of the ventricles and lasts about 0.08 s. It is depressed in ischemia (decreased blood and oxygen flow to heart muscles) and elevated in myocardial infarction.

book_ref.quote: elevated in myocardial infarction

blocks.prompt: 20 Who are blue babies? What causes their blueness?
blocks.explanation: Blue babies are abnormal newborns with blueness (cyanosis) of the skin. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, because the interatrial foramen fails to close or the ductus arteriosus fails to constrict during development, so mixed blood is supplied to the body.

book_ref.quote: They are called blue babies.

blocks.prompt: 21 Differentiate between interatrial foramen and ductus arteriosus.
blocks.explanation: Both are temporary structures of the embryonic circulation.

book_ref.quote: Interatrial foramen is a temporary opening in the embryonic heart

rows: Temporary opening in the embryonic heart between right and left atria
Temporary channel between the embryonic pulmonary artery and aorta
Normally closes during development
Normally constricts during development
Failure to close causes cyanosis
Failure to fully constrict also causes cyanosis

blocks.prompt: 22 How are capillaries formed, and what do they join to form?
blocks.explanation: Arteries divide into arterioles, which divide repeatedly into a dense network of fine branches, the capillaries. Capillaries penetrate all tissues and then join to form venules.

book_ref.quote: These vessels are formed by the division of arterioles.

blocks.prompt: 23 How do materials pass across the capillary wall?
blocks.explanation: Capillaries exchange materials between blood and tissues by diffusion or active transport. Materials pass through the endothelial cells or through the intercellular spaces of the wall; some are taken up by endocytosis and released on the other side by exocytosis.

book_ref.quote: Materials pass through the endothelial cells or through the intercellular spaces

blocks.prompt: 24 What is interstitial fluid? How is it formed?
blocks.explanation: The pressure within capillaries causes continuous leakage of fluid from blood plasma into tissues. This fluid is interstitial fluid: water with dissolved nutrients, hormones, gases, wastes and small proteins.

book_ref.quote: This fluid, known as interstitial fluid consists of water

blocks.prompt: 25 Give reason: RBCs stay in capillaries but some WBCs can leave them.
blocks.explanation: Large proteins, RBCs and platelets cannot pass through the capillary wall, so they remain within capillaries. Some WBCs can squeeze out through the intercellular spaces of the capillary wall into the tissues.

book_ref.quote: But some WBCs can squeeze out

blocks.prompt: 26 How do surrounding muscles and valves help the return of blood in veins?
blocks.explanation: The pressure generated by the contraction of surrounding muscles presses the veins and pushes blood towards the heart. Semilunar valves in veins prevent the back flow of this blood.

book_ref.quote: assists in the return of blood towards heart

blocks.prompt: 27 How is the amount of blood flowing in capillaries controlled?
blocks.explanation: By constricting or dilating the capillaries: nervous stimulation can constrict them and chemicals such as histamine can dilate them. Pre-capillary sphincters (rings of muscles at the entry of capillary loops) also regulate the flow.

book_ref.quote: Nervous stimulation can constrict capillaries

blocks.prompt: 28 Give reason: blood flow increases in a tissue whose metabolic activity rises.
blocks.explanation: When metabolic activity rises, oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide increases in the interstitial fluid. In response the circular muscles of the arterioles relax (vasodilation), increasing blood flow, which supplies more oxygen and removes more carbon dioxide.

book_ref.quote: The increased blood flow supplies more oxygen and removes more carbon dioxide.

blocks.prompt: 29 Differentiate between pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.
blocks.explanation: Both are the main pathways of blood circulation.

book_ref.quote: These are called pulmonary circulation (to and from lungs)

rows: To and from the lungs
To and from all other body parts (except lungs)
Starts from the right ventricle (pulmonary trunk)
Starts from the left ventricle (aorta)
Carries deoxygenated blood to lungs and returns oxygenated blood to heart
Supplies oxygenated blood to body and returns deoxygenated blood to heart
Ends in the left atrium (pulmonary veins)
Ends in the right atrium (vena cavae)

blocks.prompt: 30 What is the coronary sinus?
blocks.explanation: After the coronary capillaries supply the heart muscles, they unite into venules and coronary veins. The coronary veins join to form the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium; small coronary veins drain directly into the right atrium.

book_ref.quote: The coronary veins join to form a coronary sinus, which opens in right atrium.

blocks.prompt: 31 What is a portal system? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: A portal system is a circulation in which veins end in capillaries. Example: the hepatic portal system, in which the hepatic portal vein collects blood from the spleen and alimentary canal and takes it to the liver.

book_ref.quote: A portal system is a circulation in which veins end in capillaries.

blocks.prompt: 32 Give reason: blood from the alimentary canal passes through the liver before going to the heart.
blocks.explanation: This blood contains substances absorbed from the small intestine. The liver removes harmful substances from it and absorbs nutrients for storage before the blood is sent to the heart through the hepatic veins.

book_ref.quote: Liver removes harmful substances from blood

blocks.prompt: 33 Differentiate between afferent and efferent arterioles of the kidney.
blocks.explanation: Both are arterioles of the renal circulation.

book_ref.quote: The capillaries of glomeruli unite to make efferent arteriole

rows: Branch of the smaller arteries of the renal artery
Formed by the union of glomerular capillaries
Supplies blood to the nephron
Carries blood away from the glomerulus
Divides to make the capillaries of the glomerulus
Divides into peri-tubular capillaries and vasa recta

blocks.prompt: 34 Differentiate between peri-tubular capillaries and vasa recta.
blocks.explanation: Both are formed from the efferent arteriole.

book_ref.quote: peri-tubular capillaries (around nephron tubule in cortical portion of kidney)

rows: Around the nephron tubule in the cortical portion (cortex) of the kidney
Around the nephron tubule in the medulla of the kidney
One of the two sets of capillaries from the efferent arteriole
The other set of capillaries from the efferent arteriole

blocks.prompt: 35 What is pulse? Why is it felt in arteries?
blocks.explanation: Pulse is the rhythmical throbbing of arteries created by the flow of blood. It is felt in arteries because their walls are elastic and blood is forced into them at high pressure with each ventricular contraction.

book_ref.quote: The walls of arteries are elastic.

blocks.prompt: 36 What does a blood pressure reading of 120/80 mean?
blocks.explanation: The upper number (120 mm Hg) is the systolic pressure, the maximum pressure during ventricular systole. The lower number (80 mm Hg) is the diastolic pressure, the lowest pressure left in arteries before the next ventricular contraction.

book_ref.quote: Conventionally, the readings of blood pressure are expressed as 120/80.

blocks.prompt: 37 What is a sphygmomanometer? How does it show readings?
blocks.explanation: A sphygmomanometer is the instrument used for manual measurement of systolic and diastolic blood pressures. The rise and fall of its mercury column shows the readings.

book_ref.quote: rise and fall in mercury column shows the readings

blocks.prompt: 38 Differentiate between ADH and ANH in the regulation of blood pressure.
blocks.explanation: Both are hormones for long-term regulation of blood volume and pressure.

book_ref.quote: When there is stretching of the atrium by an increased blood volume

rows: Secreted by the posterior pituitary gland
Secreted by endocrine cells in the wall of the right atrium
Released when blood volume and pressure decrease
Released when the atrium is stretched by increased blood volume
Kidneys retain more water; arterioles constrict
Speeds up excretion of salts and water through urine
Raises blood volume and pressure
Lowers blood volume and pressure

blocks.prompt: 39 Differentiate between atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis.
blocks.explanation: Both are major contributors to cardiovascular disorders.

book_ref.quote: Atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis are the major contributors to cardiovascular disorders.

rows: Means deposition within arteries
Means hardening of arterial walls
Fatty materials, smooth muscle cells, cholesterol, fibrin and cellular debris accumulate; cholesterol is the prime contributor
Calcium is deposited in the arterial walls
Narrows arteries and increases the risk of thrombus and heart attack
Restricts blood flow; arteries cannot expand, so the heart works harder
Severe atherosclerosis usually leads to arteriosclerosis
Usually follows severe atherosclerosis

blocks.prompt: 40 Give reason: atherosclerosis can lead to heart attacks.
blocks.explanation: Atherosclerosis causes the narrowing of arteries and increases the risk of thrombus formation. A narrowed or blocked coronary artery cannot supply enough blood to the heart muscle, which can lead to a heart attack.

book_ref.quote: Atherosclerosis can lead to heart attacks

blocks.prompt: 41 What is an angiogram? What does a narrow artery in it indicate?
blocks.explanation: An angiogram is an X-ray picture of the contrast medium (dye) in a coronary artery, taken during coronary angiography. If clots are present in the lumen of the artery, it appears narrow in the angiogram.

book_ref.quote: Pictures (angiograms) of fluid in coronary artery are obtained.

blocks.prompt: 42 What is angina pectoris? What does it indicate?
blocks.explanation: Angina pectoris is chest pain that results during periods of stress or physical exertion when coronary arteries are narrowed by lipid build-up. It indicates that the heart's oxygen demand is greater than its delivery and a heart attack may occur in future.

book_ref.quote: chest pain, called angina pectoris, can result

blocks.prompt: 43 When is recovery from a heart attack possible?
blocks.explanation: Recovery is possible if the damaged portion of the heart is small enough that the other blood vessels of the heart can enlarge their capacity and resupply the damaged tissues.

book_ref.quote: Recovery from a heart attack is possible

blocks.prompt: 44 Give reason: lifestyle changes are needed even after a successful bypass surgery.
blocks.explanation: Bypass surgery only routes blood around the blocked area; it does not cure the underlying atherosclerosis or coronary artery disease. Smoking cessation, reducing certain fats, more physical activity and controlling blood pressure and diabetes reduce future blockages and heart attacks.

book_ref.quote: Coronary bypass surgery doesn't cure the underlying disease process

blocks.prompt: 45 What is a stent? Write its role.
blocks.explanation: A stent is an expandable stainless steel mesh tube mounted on a balloon catheter. Inflating the balloon in the narrowed artery expands the stent and the artery; the balloon is removed and the stent stays, supporting the artery walls and keeping the artery open and dilated.

book_ref.quote: The stent supports the artery walls

blocks.prompt: 46 Write the causes of hypertension.
blocks.explanation: Any abnormality in the nervous or hormonal mechanisms of blood pressure regulation may cause hypertension. Other causes are stress, obesity, high salt intake and smoking; there may also be hereditary reasons.

book_ref.quote: Other causes of hypertension include stress, obesity

blocks.prompt: 47 Differentiate between brain haemorrhage and congestive heart failure.
blocks.explanation: Both can result from chronic hypertension.

book_ref.quote: In such conditions, blood may be retained in heart and lungs.

rows: Rupture of blood vessels in the brain
Heart is unable to pump effectively
Caused by chronically elevated blood pressure
Caused by prolonged hypertension weakening the cardiac muscles
Damages the delicate structure of the brain
Blood is retained in the heart and lungs; tissue needs are not met

blocks.prompt: 48 Write the causes of thrombus formation.
blocks.explanation: Thrombus formation may be due to: (1) irritation or infection of the lining of blood vessels; (2) reduced rate of blood flow due to long periods of inactivity; (3) diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis and emphysema.

book_ref.quote: Thrombus formation may be due to

blocks.prompt: 49 What is thromboembolism?
blocks.explanation: Thromboembolism is the formation of a thrombus (clot) in a blood vessel and then its carriage to another location in the circulatory system, where it can block blood flow.

book_ref.quote: Formation of thrombus in a blood vessel and then its carriage to any other location is called thromboembolism.

blocks.prompt: 50 What is lymph? How is it formed?
blocks.explanation: Lymph is the fluid that flows in the lymphatic system. The pressure of interstitial fluid forces it into the blind-ended lymph capillaries; once interstitial fluid enters lymph capillaries, it is called lymph.

book_ref.quote: When interstitial fluid enters lymph capillaries, it is called lymph.

blocks.prompt: 51 Differentiate between lymph capillaries and blood capillaries.
blocks.explanation: Both are fine vessels in tissues.

book_ref.quote: So, larger molecules can also enter lymph capillaries.

rows: Have blind endings in interstitial fluid
Formed by arterioles and join to form venules
More permeable; larger molecules can enter
Less permeable; large proteins, RBCs and platelets stay inside
Carry lymph
Carry blood

blocks.prompt: 52 Differentiate between the right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct.
blocks.explanation: Both are the main lymph ducts formed by joining of lymph vessels.

book_ref.quote: There are two main lymph ducts i.e., right lymphatic duct and thoracic duct.

rows: Opens into the right subclavian vein
Opens into the left subclavian vein
One of the two main lymph ducts
Lymph from body tissues always flows towards it

blocks.prompt: 53 How is the flow of lymph maintained in one direction?
blocks.explanation: Lymph always flows from body tissues towards the thoracic duct. The flow is maintained by the activity of skeletal muscles, movement of viscera and breathing movements, and valves in lymph vessels prevent its back flow.

book_ref.quote: The valves present in lymph vessels prevent the back flow of lymph.

blocks.prompt: 54 What are lacteals? What enters them?
blocks.explanation: Lacteals are the branches of lymph capillaries in the villi. Fatty acids and glycerol absorbed into villus cells form triglycerides, which are coated with proteins to form chylomicrons; the chylomicrons enter the lacteals.

book_ref.quote: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the epithelial cells of villi

blocks.prompt: 55 What are lymph nodes? Where are they found in man?
blocks.explanation: Lymph nodes are masses of connective tissue with lymphocytes, present at certain spots on lymph vessels. Several afferent vessels enter a node and a single efferent vessel drains it. They are found in the neck region, axilla and groin.

book_ref.quote: At certain spots, the lymph vessels have masses of connective tissue

blocks.prompt: 56 Name the lymphoid masses of the body and write their function.
blocks.explanation: Lymphoid masses are present in the mucosa and submucosa of the alimentary canal; the larger ones are the spleen, thymus, tonsils and adenoids. They produce lymphocytes.

book_ref.quote: In addition to lymph nodes, several lymphoid masses are present

blocks.prompt: 57 Write two functions of the lymphatic system.
blocks.explanation: (1) It returns excess fluid, dissolved proteins and other substances to the blood: about three litres of fluid leaving blood capillaries daily is absorbed by lymph capillaries and returned to the bloodstream. (2) It defends the body against foreign invaders: lymph nodes filter lymph, and their lymphocytes and macrophages destroy bacteria and viruses.

book_ref.quote: Lymphatic system returns the excess fluid and dissolved proteins

blocks.prompt: 58 What is the role of the spleen?
blocks.explanation: The spleen filters blood through its macrophages and lymphocytes, which destroy foreign particles and aged RBCs. It also stores RBCs and, as a large lymphoid mass, produces lymphocytes.

book_ref.quote: Spleen filters blood through its macrophages

blocks.prompt: 59 Give reason: lymph nodes swell painfully in diseases such as mumps.
blocks.explanation: Lymph nodes contain lymphocytes and macrophages that destroy invaders. In diseases such as mumps, the painful swelling of lymph nodes is largely a result of the accumulation of dead lymphocytes and macrophages.

book_ref.quote: The painful swelling of lymph nodes in certain diseases
